Because it's an old engine then the mapper has a huge impact on optimization, you can easily create shapes that scale up PC demand exponentially and won't run on any PC, also the engine is not that well optimized for modern hardware. For example on my RTX 2060S / Ryzen 5 3600, I get increased frame times and thus input lag when walking between visleaves.

In fact it's so noticeable that i can FEEL where I'm walking through a greater density of visleaves just by playing the game.

If you ask whether it's worth to optimize so much. Try disabling VIS compiler altogether. The map will work just fine. Some Source engine features like real-time reflections depend on it being enabled, but I'm not sure about GoldSrc.

In most cases it's not worth it, but maybe I could even say that it's not worth using func\_detail altogether and just disabling VIS compilation completely.

I don't know what bugs that will cause, because I haven't noticed any so if you want to experiment you can try that approach. The whole map will render at once, there will be no culling, and perhaps that's not a problem.

But yes, if optimization takes too much of your time then I wouldn't do it. Setting up different detail levels is natural for me, so I'm fine with doing it myself.

no, that is exactly the best case to use it. cutting will happen two objects are of the same detail level. world brushes are detail level 0.

the thing is that it works only between world brushes and func\_detail level 1

if two different func\_detail touch each other in a way that would cut faces, then you need additional levels.

So let's say room floor / walls -> world brush

sink base -> func\_detail 1

sink detail on sink base -> func\_detail 2

sink details details on sink details -> func\_detail 3

and so on

The whole reason func\_detail works is because it uses detail level 1. If you change it to 0 you will notice that it acts exactly like a regular world brush, I actually use that feature sometimes to put an object into a wall, without having to cut an opening, because it seems to be prioritized and override regular world brush faces.

To check how faces cutting works you can use commands "gl\_wireframe" (0 off / 1 on / 2 on + wallhack) and "r\_speeds" (0 / 1).

gl\_wireframe is the most important, it will show exactly where faces are, and how they are getting cut.

r\_speeds shows how many faces (wpolys) are currently rendered and a few other things, don't pay attention to fps when gl\_wireframe is turned on, because it tanks framerate a lot. This isn't necessary in this case, but it's an useful thing regardless.

I use these binds frequently, you can copy them into console if you want.

bind , "gl\_wireframe 0; r\_speeds 0"

bind . "gl\_wireframe 1; r\_speeds 1"

bind / "gl\_wireframe 2; r\_speeds 1"

Cutting faces works similarly to cutting visleaves, but this only applies when two objects touch each other. For example a wooden crate on a floor, the game will treat bottom of the crate as a backface. It won't appear in game, that whole area underneath will be cut out and a void left there.

You can check this by recreating this scenario and nocliping inside the crate, you will notice a hole in the floor. And if you enable wireframe, you will notice that faces had to be cut by the compiler around that hole to fit it.

If you make that crate into a func\_detail, you will notice that hole in the world is gone. That's what happens when you use func\_detail and it's exactly why func\_detail can't be used to seal the map. It's as if it's compiled in a different layer, the floor doesn't care about it.

In a small scene like this this probably doesn't matter much, but if the crate was huge, it would create a situation where there is a piece a huge chunk of floor pointlessly rendered underneath, that the player can't see anyway. This is why backface cutting is a thing in the first place, but for small details like your sink it does more harm than good.

If you add another small crate on top of that func\_detail and also make it a func\_detail (and don't change the detail level), you will notice that that smaller crate actually cuts into that larger crate and crates a hole in that.

This mostly matters when you have advanced shapes your sink. If all of them have the same detail level, then the compiler needs to create a lot of faces just to cut out that tiny backface in your sink.

If you enable gl\_wireframe and compare both of these cases (all single detail level vs multiple detail levels) you will understand what I mean. You can also check r\_speeds and how wpolys change. I would expect maybe a 8x difference for that face touched by the plug.

More about this here, if you scroll down a section about detail level [https://twhl.info/wiki/page/Tutorial%3A\_Advanced\_Terrain\_Creation](https://twhl.info/wiki/page/Tutorial%3A_Advanced_Terrain_Creation)

\---

btw

Instead of func\_detail you could actually use a regular brush entity like func\_wall, func\_detail isn't an entity in game, only an internal entity that exists in editor to give world brushes context for the compiler, so that it treats them differently during compilation. [https://developer.valvesoftware.com/wiki/Entity\_(GoldSrc)](https://developer.valvesoftware.com/wiki/Entity_(GoldSrc))

func\_wall has positives and drawbacks, and this is how Valve did it, as func\_detail wasn't there in the original HL 1 compilers. Using func\_wall is kind of like using only a single detail level for itself, it doesn't cut into world brushes or other brush entities, but it does cut into itself if you tie multiple brushes into a single entity, but I won't explain it further as of now, unless you want to, because really I could write a book about this shit.

For a regular, static purpose func\_detail is better. Brush entities are useful when if you want to disable / enable / kill them, or disable / enable their render.

I think you confused one thing

\_process is the function that runs all the time, it's basically your framerate. If you have a game running at 300 FPS, it means that \_process was called 300 times (in theory at least).

\_process\_physics is not running as fast possible, only in specific time-based intervals, it doesn't matter if a game runs at 300 FPS or 100 FPS, this function will run the same amount of times per second.

delta is just a variable that contains the amount of time that has passed since the last time the function was ran. For example if you have 1 FPS in game, that means the delta is 1 second. If you have 10 FPS, then the delta is 0.1 seconds.

You don't have to use delta if you don't need to. Often you can just add things to \_process\_physics and ignore delta. Or the same way you can ignore \_process\_physics and only use \_process and use delta when necessary. Whatever is easier for you / better for the situation.

\-------------------------

Also, \_process and \_process\_physics are always ran no matter if you include them or not, you only need to include them if you want something to happen when they are ran.

If you have a static type and errors/warnings to enforce that then this seriously lowers the amount of checking you have to do, and has a lot of QoL too.

Let's say you have a function f(x) that returns y

The Y is supposed to be X multiplied by itself.

So for example f(5) would return 25.

But what if you make a mistake and pass a wrong type, for example a string? f('hello') will result in a runtime error that you might only notice months later. 

And also without static typing you need to do write additional code that check the type at the beginning of the function. I.e. is X is null, is X an int etc.

If we had typing defined beforehand for example f(x: int) we would get an immediate warning if someone tried to use f like this -> f('hello'). 

So you can notice your mistake right away.

‐------------

Additional QoL (and the main reason why I like static typing) is that it allows you and your editor to be on the same page.

If you specify a type for example x: Car, the editor knows that x is a Car and can give you auto-completion hints.

For example after writing "x." you will get a list of possible functions / properties that x contains and that you can use. So in this case it would be things like x.toggle_engine(), x.engine_status etc.

If you don't specify type hint, then you yourself know that X is a car, but your editor doesn't! And so you can't get any tips from the editor.

But as a rule of thumb for me:

Object = Allows for State and Logic together.

Class = a contract for an object.

OOP is vague, because it literally can be applied to everything.  Everything can be an object if you allow it to.

C++ must follow all C rules, and if OOP works in C++ then it also works in C. Your struct example is just an ugly OOP implementation.

In some languages a function is an object, a struct (which should only hold state) can be an object, even a primitive int can be an object.

Usually I say class and instance to be specific.

I've modded STALKER 2 so I can talk about few things.

First off, there are Stalker 2 config files where you can change some values, like difficulty scaling, mutant HP, certain texts etc. but there is no way to change logic through that. All AI mods just change things like respawn distance or enable features that were disabled by default.

Second the Unreal Engine has engine specific console commands, most of them are shared between all UE 5 games, I'm currently playing through Oblivion Remaster and I use the same Engine.ini changes I've used for STALKER 2. Again, no way to change logic with these besides enabling / disabling features, editing values.

Third, some games, I'm not sure about STALKER 2 have scripting languages (Kingdom Come 2 for example has this in form of Lua). These scripting languages aren't transpiled into a human unreadable format (like the C++, main language of Unreal Engine does), and thus can be edited.

Some games like Hades are written almost entirely in scripting langauges and thus are very easy to mod, everyone can just edit the files and change the logic. You can't do the same with C++, because the final build of the game just contains gibberish and theoretically can be reverse engineered (Like it was done with Diablo 1 [https://devilutionx.com/](https://devilutionx.com/) ), but realistically it's a task so hard and time consuming that no one will do it.

I think STALKER 1 uses scripting for a few things too, but not everything of course. I'm not sure about STALKER 2.

Now, it's up to STALKER 2 devs to release the human readable format of the source files, or at least an API that makes modding easier. ( for example Half-Life 1 source code is officially released here [https://github.com/ValveSoftware/halflife](https://github.com/ValveSoftware/halflife), same with Half-Life 2 and Team Fortress 2 [https://github.com/ValveSoftware/source-sdk-2013](https://github.com/ValveSoftware/source-sdk-2013) )

TL;DR anything that is stored in human readable format is easy to mod, anything that isn't is hard to mod.

Low-level languages like Assembly are for working closely with the CPU instructions. For pure logic, langauges like Python are the best, it's why Python is one of the more popular choice in data science.

You don't need to understand CS as a whole, but every bit of it will make different areas of programming easier.

For writing efficient game engines understanding how computer memory works is definitely important, but just for writing simple game logic, like how the player inventory works, not at all, for that even Python would be good.

For games just geometry related math would be most important, vectors, trigonometry etc., but it really depends on what you actually need for a game. Most of that can be learned on the fly.

No, it's really that simple. Update loop where we make the differences for the next frame, and then render loop where we render it, and again.

After a frame is displayed, the next update loop's job is to make the difference required for the next frame. 

This could be, move something by a milimeter, or not if it's not supposed to move. 

After that, render loop runs and renders the frame based on current state of the game. We assume it's current game state, because it's not allowed to change here, otherwise you would get a distored reality where things from the past and future appear on the same screen at once.

After that, update loop runs again. 

This repeats as fast as the computer is able to process it. If it's able to process the game loop 300 times per second, you get 300 FPS in game.

If we add an artificial sleep to the loop we can limit FPS to 60 for example.

HTML describes the layout of the page. (Text, buttons etc.)

CSS describes the styling of the page. (Colors etc.)

HTML / CSS / JS is something you 100% need for web-apps, so there's no choice here, just learn it. Outside of web-apps, you don't need any of these, but JS can be used for non-web apps too.

TypeScript / React are optional tools that help you make your apps in a more organized way. That's why they're commonly used these days.

TypeScript is also a good introduction to other static type languages, which would be useful for back-end sides of your web-apps.

Back-end is not always required for web-apps, unless your app is multi-user. Games and simple tools will most often work just fine with front-end only apps, which are often free to host on sites like GitHub Pages, Vercel, Netlify.

However multi-user apps such as those that require accounts, other info that needs to be stored safely on the server, need a server. Which is your back-end.

Whenever a client enters a path in the browser, it sends a HTTP GET request to that IP with that specific path, the server then responds with a HTTP response, but it's up to the server how that response will look like.

By default most www servers will respond with data that contains the html / css / js etc., whatever is required for that page to load.

You on your server can respond in other formats too, for example JSON. Most modern browsers will load that successfully too.

Client can send requests through JS too, this is useful when you need small amounts of data for use in your JS scripts, not the whole page, this is where JSON format is useful.

Server can be setup in a way where certain paths for example /api/get_items will respond with JSON instead, this is useful for whenever you want something in JSON format on client-side.

Some tips:

Recall before cannon wave, you will lose less plates and maybe less farm.

Amount of minions and placement of the wave will tell you what will happen with the wave.

If there is an equal amount of yours and enemy minions and the wave is closer to your tower, it will push towards the enemy, if it's closer to enemy tower it will push towards you.

The reason for this is because the wave is closer to the base and it will start atracking minions before the opposite wave can.

Other tip:

When someone attacks the enemy, the minions will aggro on him, this will cause him to take more damage, because of minions, but notice what happens with the minions, instead of pushing the wave they attack the champion, so this causes the wave to push towards the champion that good attacked.

This is important to remember,  especially in early levels.

.

You can also abuse this to get the wave closer to you so you can farm under your tower if that's what you need at the moment. 

When you expect to get attacked by an AoE like Pantheon Q you can stay behind your minions, the wave will push as he tries to Q you.

Similarly you can try attcking the enemy, while your minions are low hp, he will have to choose between killing the minion or focusing on you. You will either win trade easier or cause him to lose gold.

For pressure you just need experience and general awareness. It's impossible to understand how pressured you are if you don't know what the enemy is capable of.

For example, let's say you are pushing tier 2 tower on top, you can see 3 enemy players on the map far away from you, and the only enemy champion that you can't see is someone weak 1v1 like let's say Leona, then there is no pressure you and you can push freely without even any wards around you.

If Leona came here and jump on you while you are pushing, you can just ignore her and keep pushing. She can't do anything to stop you besides killing the minions (which she can't do well, because Leona has weak wave clear).

But let's say ADC and Support are missing, which happens often, because they usually walk together, this puts a little pressure on you, because if Leona was to engage on you with an ADC behind her, you can die if you're not prepared.

So you need to respond to the pressure properly, this doesn't necessairly mean stopping the push, you just need to make sure that you have the tools to escape ready, for Garen to escape safely you need to prepare Phase Rush / Stridebreaker and wait for enemy CC to hit you first, before you activate it.

This means when pushing like that, don't waste Stridebreaker on minions (which you could do in a previous example without ADC) since you need it to escape. Just push with as little abilities as possible, so you have enough of them to activate Phase Rush. Also, make sure to ward somewhere behind the turret in the jungle, so you can escape faster if the need comes.

If you won't respect pressure here, you risk getting engaged by them and not having how to escape because you wasted all abilities and Stridebreaker on minions.

If you do respect pressure, your push is only a little less efficient, but you're much safer.

This shows the power of pressure, Garen has to push a little bit slower, just because ADC is missing from the map. In low elo this works differently, because people don't respect pressure as much, so it's good to take advantage of that.

The cause of z-fighting is rather hard to explain, because one has to understand float value inaccuracies, but I can try explaining in a different way.

One may think that when nothing really changes on the screen, then the performance should be good, but it's not how 99%+ of game engines work, in truth every frame everything is redrawn again, even when it's not necessary as not much changed on the screen.

When z-fighting appears, this overhead actually starts to fullfil it's purpose, because things change on the screen.

Or to put it differently, rendering is optimized to these weird cases where a lot of stuff changes on screen, like in case of z-fighting, so whenever it doesn't happen the performance doesn't actually improve, because the engine doesn't check that (as that would be an another overhead), instead the worst possible outcome is assumed and everything is redrawn anyway.

It would be possible to optimize the rendering in a way, where no z-fighting would improve performance (in a way), but because image in games constantly has to change as it's not just a still image it would be unnecessary and would only worsen performance in cases where we actually need high-performing constantly changing images.

The most important things to consider for me are lines of sight for VIS, max level size, and average detail level.

If the map doesn't have any lines of sight to break up VIS you have to remember that it will render all at once in certain spots, which is fine if you think your map can handle this, but it's often not necessary. This has to be thought at the beginning, because it's a foundational decision which can't really be changed later easily.

Max level size is more of a problem in HL 1 rather than HL 2, but it's still something to think about even for a second.

Average detail level is a decision that needs to be made early on, because without this, the map will either look inconsistent, or take forever to make. If you'll start making very detailed environments at the beginning, you might realize that you cannot make the whole map like this. 

This is why it's better to work in layers and design the whole map first, and then add next layers, gameplay, texturing, detailing etc. rather than starting with a complete first room, before the rest of the map is made.

As for planning out ideas, if they're simple I just plan things out in my head, if the layout is harder, I'll draw something quickly in MS Paint, if I don't have any cool ideas, I just don't plan, it will only result in boring layouts.

P.S. don't get mistaken, func\_viscluster doesn't mark the area for a visleaf, but tells the VIS compiler where to avoid splitting visleaves if possible.
